title: Trump Invites Xi to a Show. What Did the US Get in Return?
dek: This state visit has almost no substantive agenda — it is pure symbolism and optics. The question is not whether something goes wrong, but what the US is trading symbolism for in substance. So far: nothing.
why: The first half covers the summit and US-China relations; the middle and later sections on China after Xi and fifty years since Mao's death are denser with information and worth listening to.
who: Founders and investors watching the direction of US-China relations, especially those who need to judge policy uncertainty and supply chain, semiconductor and AI regulation risk.
skip: The opening chit-chat about state dinner performers and divorce betting odds can be skipped.

points.h: This visit has no substantive agenda at all
points.body: Gewirtz's judgment is that this state visit has "there is not a very deep substantive agenda at all." Trump invited Xi mainly because he wants to put on a show, wants the pomp and the cameras, and wants to push issues like the Iran war out of the news. For Beijing, this actually makes them less nervous — because if it were a more confrontational meeting, they would be more anxious. But Gewirtz flags two things: Trump himself is extremely unpredictable, and Beijing has internalized that; and Beijing, watching the chaos in Washington, sees the American president himself often in a position they would never want Xi to be in — going to the wrong place, being photographed in unflattering images, being pressed by reporters. So the real question is not whether someone deliberately sets a trap, but whether things slip into the very scenario they are desperate to avoid.

points.h: Symbolism for substance: where is the trade
points.body: Gewirtz characterizes this visit as "we are in a space of symbolism and optics." He says that in US-China relations, trading symbolism for substance is itself a reasonable play: give Beijing the pomp and cameras it craves, and get back something concretely useful to Americans and American interests. That was the model for US relations with the Soviets during the Cold War and after — the US gave symbolism, legitimacy and that handshake photo, and got a concession in return on a Third World country or a nuclear issue. But the problem this time is that the Trump administration does not even seem to have attempted to design a set of "deliverables." Gewirtz says "it doesn't even seem like they're trying." So what to watch is not where things go wrong, but "where is the trade happening."

points.h: The direction of concessions has been flipped entirely
points.body: Gewirtz points to a counterintuitive dynamic: concessions the US might once have given China have now been flipped into "gifts" from China to the US. Pomp and cameras were what Beijing wanted, but in Washington they are treated as Xi's visit being a concession to the US. The same flip happens on advanced semiconductors: the US used not to sell these things, and opening up products like the H200 would have been a huge concession; now, if Beijing agrees to buy, many in Washington would see it as Beijing conceding to Trump. Gewirtz says this flip keeps recurring, and the reason it matters is not to score the administration but because it reflects what happens when the power gap in superpower competition narrows — very small differences, personal dynamics, can produce much larger displacements in the overall strategic picture.

points.h: US-China relations are also K-shaped, held up by the upper leg
points.body: Gewirtz uses the "K-shaped" idea for US-China relations: one upward leg is the leader-level channel — dense exchanges of visits, friendship, cameras; one downward leg is the reality of competition and the actions parts of both governments keep taking. The system is currently held up by the upward leg, but it is very fragile. He stresses the metaphor is not just a parallel analogy: saying "truce" or "detente" sounds too static, like a state already reached, but US-China relations are actually quite dynamic and quite unstable, moving in two directions at once. He applies the same K-shaped logic to China's economy — manufacturing and AI are flying, real estate and consumer demand are struggling, the upward leg is pulling the whole system forward, and the question is whether it can keep holding as the K widens.

points.h: The bipartisan consensus on China policy has shattered
points.body: Gewirtz argues that Trump changed the tone of America's China discussion in the 2016 election and became the symbol and standard-bearer of that turn; but now, after helping create that turn, he has helped destroy or transform it. He cites David Feith's article in the Reagan Institute on "a new cold war in an age of doubt" — that great rethink on China was not as great as many assumed. Gewirtz's conclusion: if the political dynamics are more complicated than imagined and the bipartisan consensus some people talk about does not exist, then this is a moment of "incredible fluidity." He says he has no confidence in the medium-term direction of either Democratic or Republican China policy, and Beijing has no confidence either.

points.h: Chinese officials cannot talk about risks they have no solution for
points.body: Gewirtz offers a different read on how the US should interpret Chen Yixin's article. On the surface, Americans are panicking about existential risk and China is panicking about regime security, and that is right. But he says: heads of American AI model companies can talk at length about risks they have no solution for, and all of them do; China's minister of state security cannot. In China, when you point out a risk in public, you are simultaneously saying "we the Communist Party see it, we will handle it, we have a solution." So the real question is: should we treat what we can see from Beijing as everything, or acknowledge that there is more in the system that we cannot see. He gives an example from 25 years ago — Americans then predicted the internet would cause regime change in China, Clinton said that was like nailing Jell-O to the wall, and Beijing really did nail the Jell-O to the wall, namely the firewall.

points.h: Beijing has not decided how to regulate open models
points.body: Gewirtz says that around Xi's speech and Chen Yixin's article, the outside world has already been through several cycles of excitement and interpretation, but Beijing has still not given the single most important thing: how it plans to regulate open weight models spreading globally — models that carry both risk and strategic benefit for Beijing. He calls this "the trillion dollar question." Both speeches can be read as pointing in some direction, but the decision has not been made. His guess is that this is because Beijing itself has not decided, because things are changing too fast and the trade-offs are too large. He contrasts the Trump administration: it did not make a decision until Mythos came out, and then made another when Fable came out.

points.h: What to prepare for is not China's decline but Xi's decline
points.body: Gewirtz says that a few years ago the "peak China" debate asked whether to start preparing for China's decline, and now most people think China's economy is at least for the moment on a relatively sustainable path. But he thinks the real question is not that, but "do we need to prepare for Xi Jinping's decline" — because people die, and modern Chinese history tells us that leaders in power for a long time change with age, certain obsessions become more prominent, behavior changes. By "prepare" he does not mean the departure itself, but acknowledging uncertainty: the outside world has treated Xi's tenure as fairly predictable, because since taking power in 2012 and 2013 he laid out a set of goals and largely pursued them. But he stresses change could absolutely be for the worse from America's perspective — "That doesn't mean he's going to mellow."

points.h: No one predicted the post-Xi era accurately
points.body: Gewirtz says much of his academic career has studied the decisive turning points of modern China: Mao's death, the turn around 1989, WTO accession and the transformation that followed. He notes these moments are often described as elite power struggles or high-level changes at the center of Beijing, but they are also — perhaps more so — transformations of Chinese society, driven not only from the top down but also from the bottom up. On China after Xi, he lists several scenarios: linear continuity, more nationalist or more confrontational, or even more openness or liberalization. But he says the clearest trend in these historical moments is that "nobody got it right" — no one accurately predicted what would happen, change during transitions is fast, and not everything changes on day one. To those confidently predicting what China will look like on day one after Xi, he offers a request: predict six months and one year out with the same confidence.
